advisor.summary: Section 402A(c)(4) lets a participant convert vested pre-tax 401(k) balances to a designated Roth account inside the plan — including, since the ATRA expansion, amounts not otherwise distributable. The converted amount is ordinary income in the conversion year at rates that are, post-OBBBA, permanent and known; everything after grows tax-free with no lifetime RMDs. The strategy is deliberate bracket-filling: convert exactly enough to absorb the low brackets in a genuine income valley, or in a year a large deduction — defined benefit funding, cost segregation, a big charitable year — has crushed taxable income. Because TCJA repealed recharacterization, the election is irrevocable; sizing waits for a near-final Q4 projection and must price the AGI-driven cliffs (SALT-cap phase-down, QBI thresholds, NIIT, IRMAA) that push the true marginal cost above the nominal bracket.
mechanics: The plan must offer designated Roth accounts and permit in-plan conversions; §402A(c)(4)(E) reaches amounts not otherwise distributable, and Notices 2010-84 and 2013-74 supply the operating rules — solo 401(k) documents vary widely, so read the document before promising anything.

The converted amount is ordinary income in the conversion year under the §408A(d)(3) framework; no 10% early-distribution penalty applies at conversion, but amounts withdrawn within five years can trigger penalty recapture.
There is no income limit and no dollar cap — the ceiling is bracket tolerance, so the right size fills the target bracket and stops.
The best conversion years are often manufactured: a defined benefit funding year, a cost segregation year, or a genuine income valley lets pre-tax dollars convert at 10–22% instead of 32–37%.

Conversion income raises AGI, which can phase down the OBBBA SALT cap, squeeze the QBI thresholds, expose other income to NIIT, and set IRMAA surcharges two years out — fill brackets net of these cliffs, not gross.
Recharacterization is repealed (TCJA), so the election is irrevocable — execute in Q4 against near-final numbers, or split the conversion across December and January to straddle the uncertainty.

authority.note: Authorizes in-plan Roth rollovers; subparagraph (E) extends them to amounts not otherwise distributable.
The conversion-inclusion framework — ordinary income above basis — that the plan rules incorporate.
The Q&A guidance on in-plan Roth rollovers: taxation, withholding, and the five-year recapture rule.
Implements the expansion to nondistributable amounts and sets out the plan-amendment requirements.
Made the TCJA rate structure permanent — conversions now lock in known rates rather than racing a sunset — and created the SALT-cap phase-down that conversion income can trigger.

requirements: A plan document with designated Roth accounts and an in-plan conversion feature — amend it in if absent.
Vested pre-tax balances worth converting, plus cash outside the plan for the tax; paying it from converted dollars guts the math.
A reliable year-end projection, because the election cannot be undone.
A low-bracket year, or an offsetting-deduction year, to convert into.
risks: Irrevocability is the headline risk: the TCJA repealed recharacterization, so an overshoot is a permanent overpayment — which is why sizing waits for near-final Q4 numbers.

The AGI cascade can push the true marginal cost well above the nominal bracket: SALT-cap phase-down above the OBBBA MAGI threshold, QBI phase-outs, NIIT on investment income, and IRMAA surcharges for clients 63 and older.
Paying the conversion tax from plan assets — or with penalty-bearing early money — destroys the arbitrage; outside cash only.
The Notice 2010-84 five-year recapture rule surprises under-59½ clients who tap converted amounts early.
Converting in an ordinary high-income year at 32–37% usually just prepays tax at top rates — the value lies in the timing, not the conversion itself.
stateNotes: States that conform to federal AGI pick up the conversion income automatically, so the sizing should include a state-level bracket check — and a client planning a move to a no-tax state may prefer to defer conversions until after the move.
No PTET interaction — the conversion is participant-level income, not entity income a pass-through entity tax election could absorb.

Missouri conforms through RSMo §143.121, so converted amounts are Missouri income in the conversion year; the state's comparatively low individual rate keeps the cost of an in-state conversion modest.
reviewChecklist: Plan document confirmed (or amended) to allow designated Roth accounts and in-plan conversions before any amount is promised.
Year-end projection covers every planned deduction and the AGI cliffs — SALT phase-down, QBI, NIIT, IRMAA — before the amount is set.
Outside cash earmarked for the tax, with Q4 estimates or withholding adjusted to avoid underpayment penalties.
Client sign-off on irrevocability obtained in writing.
After execution: 1099-R reconciled and the plan's five-year clocks documented in the file.

client.teaser: Pay the tax on retirement money in your cheapest year — then never again.
client.headline: Convert retirement money in a low-tax year and lock the savings in
plainEnglish: Your pre-tax retirement account carries a built-in tax bill. The IRS just has not collected it yet. Every withdrawal in retirement gets taxed. And in your seventies, the government forces money out on its schedule, not yours.

A conversion flips the deal. You pick an amount, pay tax on it now, and move it to the tax-free side of your plan. From then on it grows with no tax and no forced withdrawals. The skill is picking the right year — a year your income dips, or a year a big deduction has pushed your rate way down.

We size the amount with care. Enough to fill your low tax brackets, and not a dollar more. One thing to know going in: once it is done, it cannot be undone. That is why we run it late in the year, when the numbers are nearly final.
client.analogy: Your future tax bill is like a debt that must be paid in some year. We pick the year it goes on sale.
benefits: Withdrawals of converted money are tax-free for life
No forced withdrawals later — you control the timing
Pairs with big-deduction years to convert at bargain rates
Shrinks the fully taxed forced withdrawals waiting in your seventies
steps: WE spot the low-tax window and confirm your plan allows conversions.
WE size the exact amount that fills your cheap brackets and stops there.
YOU set aside outside cash for the tax bill — never plan money.
WE execute late in the year and repeat in each future low-rate year.
clientCommitments: Keep outside cash ready for the conversion tax
Hold the decision until we have near-final year-end numbers
Leave converted money alone — early withdrawals can trigger penalties
